name: Daria Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, 58, lead developer at a tech company that tracks blood-bank stock. I have a master's degree and know the inventory rules well, but I still ask the nurse to sign an issue slip before I move a unit on the screen. I have never used AI tools. My partner teaches full-time, our son is grown, and we have a car loan to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the blood bank a unit is available only when its label and the nurse's issue slip agree. I lead software for a tech company's blood-inventory system and have never used AI; I keep the signed batch ledger beside the release screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, I expect my senior job and our wages to continue. I have a master's degree, typical lead pay, a partner teaching full-time and five months of expenses saved; there are some other software firms near us, though we still have a car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reconciling blood-unit location bugs against the batch ledger. We'd pay another 100 monthly toward the car loan while both wages hold and at least four months of expenses remain saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this version. A unit shown in the wrong fridge can cost a nurse time that a patient does not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where was the missing blood unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen put two units in Fridge B, but the signed issue slip showed one had gone to theatre. I corrected the inventory after checking with the nurse, not from the screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son pay the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son lives independently. We are glad he visits, but his salary is not part of our car-loan plan.

I'd keep **fridge locations** correct before a nurse asks for stock.
think: I expect **two wages** and my lead post to hold under mild AI.
I have **five months saved** while paying a car loan.
do: Keep **reconciling unit locations** with signed nurse slips and batch ledger.
Pay **100 extra monthly** on car loan only while both wages hold and four months remain saved.
feel: **Calm** about current wages, careful with blood availability.

fieldNote: **Two steady wages** and five months saved support calm despite a manageable car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write inventory code and answer stock requests, but a blood unit must not be called available from an old screen. I would make the blood-bank staff show us where the unit actually is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead experience is valuable, yet the firm could combine maintenance teams and reduce my paid hours. Five months saved helps, but my partner's teaching wage alone will not cover every bill and the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper list of wrong-fridge cases and take it to the weekly blood-bank review. We'd stop extra car-loan payments if my hours fall, keeping the four-month reserve; I'd ask the blood bank whether any paid traceability posts exist, but change jobs only for a real opening with signed household pay covering housing, food and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours and about an unavailable unit being promised to a ward. I am not letting an AI tool change live blood records without the blood bank's verified checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which slip details matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre issue slip had the unit number, time and nurse signature. If any of those are missing, I want the blood unit marked uncertain, not available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the loan overpayment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would keep the normal car instalment in the budget. The extra amount can stop as soon as my paid hours are reduced.

I'd keep **uncertain units** out of the available count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write blood-bank code before handling robots arrive around 2031. A nurse still needs a person to correct a wrong unit location.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead post as soon as cheaper code covers the routine checks. My partner's teaching wage and five months saved would cover a search, but the car loan and our living costs still need income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the hospital blood bank and three nearby software firms about actual paid stock-audit or safety-test vacancies, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only signed work whose combined wages cover housing, food, car payments and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using the reserve and ask the lender before missing an instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the bigger wage. A ledger full of blood units is not a list of jobs I can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an anonymised theatre issue-slip correction to another employer, with patient and nurse names removed. It demonstrates why the unit had to be moved out of Fridge B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which pay timing matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would check the new role's hours against the teaching day. If the job has a gap in paid weeks, the stated annual salary may not cover the monthly car payment.

I'd check **real signed vacancies** before naming a fallback.

I cannot cover **car loan and bills** indefinitely from savings.

fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches inventory code before 2031 handling robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us reduce fixed bills before thinking AI reaches blood-bank code. Handling robots come around 2034, but my work is already on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot count on five years of lead wages, so the car loan is the one bill we can shrink while we are earning. I would not put our four-month emergency reserve into a lump-sum payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking theatre issue slips and ask the lender for an updated car-loan payoff schedule. We'd pay 180 extra monthly only while both wages hold and four months stay saved, stopping the extra if either income falls; in the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid development if offered or seek a signed local role whose combined wages cover housing, food, remaining car payments and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the lead post, but I can make the monthly bill smaller without gambling the reserve. I won't tell my partner the car is paid off until the lender's statement says it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will the lender schedule show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The updated schedule should show how each extra payment changes the balance. I would compare it with the emergency account every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if either wage falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants the normal instalment budgeted even while we pay more. If either wage falls, we preserve four months cash before trying to finish the loan early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 could take me to 68, but thinking AI reaches blood-bank code before handling robots around 2039. A paper issue slip should remain legible when I am no longer writing the fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today we have two wages and five months saved, so the car loan is manageable. I have not checked our retirement amounts, and I cannot promise either the car or my job will be finished on a particular date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the issue-slip checks and pay 100 extra monthly toward the car while both wages hold and four months stay saved, then request retirement and lender statements each year. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified income covers housing, food, remaining car payments and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid work without counting our son's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant employment, but current bills are paid. I would rather read a balance than announce the car and my career are both finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the archive show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The archive should show the unit number, signed theatre issue and corrected fridge location with names removed. Another worker ought to see why the screen was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son pay the car loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son can visit when he wishes. He is building his own life, and his salary does not belong on our retirement sheet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could cut lead inventory work before a hospital or nearby company offers paid testing. Written notice, real job pay and an early lender conversation would help us keep the car payment current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a blood unit can be counted twice just because the screen says so. A nurse has to find the physical unit; the code cannot donate blood to a patient.

headlineQuote: A nurse has to find the physical unit; the code cannot donate blood to a patient.
portrait: Daria, **58**, leads blood-bank inventory software after a master's degree and checks units against signed nurse slips.
Her **typical lead pay**, partner's teaching wage, five-month reserve and some nearby firms make a car loan manageable today.
She has **never used AI** and protects a four-month reserve while weighing any paid traceability opening.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; signed replacement wages must cover housing, food, car payments and travel.
At five years, she makes **extra car principal** conditional on two wages and four months saved; retirement needs verified figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her larger wage before another paid stock-audit role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid vacancies and lender contact before arrears would help.
